hook: Drop a hot pan in a sink of cold water and it hisses, then goes quiet. A few minutes later the pan and the water are at the same lukewarm temperature, and they stay that way. What happened is a crowd of fast particles nudging slow ones until, on average, nobody is faster than anyone else.

prereq.q: Temperature is a measure of the particles'
prereq.why: Higher temperature means the particles move faster on average.

prereq.q: In an exothermic process, the surroundings
prereq.why: Energy leaves the system and enters the surroundings, so they warm.

figure.caption: Energy passes by collisions from the faster particles of the hot block to the slower particles of the cold block until their average speeds match.

chain.cause: Two objects at different temperatures touch
chain.effect: particles at the boundary collide, the faster ones from the hot object with the slower ones from the cold object

chain.cause: In those collisions, faster particles usually lose energy and slower ones gain it
chain.effect: energy flows from the hotter object to the cooler one

chain.cause: The hot object loses energy and the cold one gains it
chain.effect: their temperatures move toward each other
energy passes equally both ways, so there is no net flow: thermal equilibrium

chain.cause: Energy is conserved in an isolated system
chain.effect: energy lost by the hot object equals energy gained by the cold one

ideas: Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference; it always flows from warmer to cooler.
At the particle level, heat transfer happens by collisions: fast particles speed up slow ones.
Thermal equilibrium: equal temperatures, no net energy flow, though collisions continue.
In an insulated (isolated) system, energy lost by one object = energy gained by the other.
The final temperature lies between the starting temperatures.

misconception.wrong: Ice cools a drink by giving it cold.
misconception.right: Cold is not a thing that moves. The drink cools because energy flows out of it into the colder ice.

summary: When objects at different temperatures touch, collisions pass energy from the faster particles of the hotter object to the slower particles of the cooler one. The flow continues until both reach the same temperature, thermal equilibrium. In an insulated system, the energy one object loses equals the energy the other gains.
